title: Why beating a stronger player earns you 29 points, not 16
description:
Elo ratings first predict the game: every 400 points of gap makes the stronger player 10 times the favourite, so a 1,500 player facing a 1,900 is expected to score 1 game in 11 (0.09). After the game, the rating moves by K times (result minus prediction): with K = 32, a win is 32 x 0.91 = 29 points, and the opponent loses exactly 29. Beating an equal is 32 x 0.5 = 16; beating a 1,100 is only 3, and losing to them costs 29. The US Chess Federation adopted Arpad Elo's system in 1960 and FIDE in 1970.

Numbers checked in code: the Elo formulas with K = 32 (the classic setting for players under 2100), plus 200,000 simulated games confirming the 1-in-11 upset rate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elo_rating_system

beats.say: Beat an equal: plus 16. Beat a giant: plus 29.
That's not a bonus for being brave. It's the size of the surprise.
This is Elo's system, chess ratings since 1960. You're fifteen hundred. They're nineteen hundred.
First, predict. Every 400 points of gap makes the stronger player 10 times the favourite. So you're expected to score 1 game in 11.
You win. Take what happened, 1, minus what was predicted, 0.09. That's 0.91 of surprise.
Times 32. Plus 29 for you, and they lose exactly 29.
But what if you beat someone you were supposed to beat?
Against an eleven hundred, a win gets you 3 points. A loss costs you 29.
Your rating isn't a score. It's a prediction, and it only moves when it's wrong.
So you're seventeen hundred and you beat a fifteen hundred. How many points do you get?
